lignes.texte: Right now, millions of families are blindly walking into a financial crisis.
To chase the American Dream, they’re signing over 50% of their entire paycheck
just to keep a roof over their heads. It should be a red flag. A reason for banks
to ring the alarm bells. But corporate housebuilders have found a workaround.
By acting as the builder, broker and shadow lender,
these mega-corporations are masking the real cost of home ownership with artificial teaser
rates. They’re luring middle class families into ticking debt bombs.
And the suburbs are one rate reset from exploding.
For anyone working in the housing market, the 2008 financial crisis still makes them wake up
in a cold sweat. The massive housing collapse was triggered by toxic loans given to owners who had
little hope of ever paying off their house. The resulting domino effect not only caused an untold
number of people to lose their homes, but led to the complete collapse of multiple high-profile
banks and investment firms. The shockwaves were felt across the global economy. In the slow,
agonizing recovery that followed, people vowed to never make these same mistakes again.
So, they found a whole new bunch of mistakes to make.
For a long time, the tighter regulations on the housing market made it look like buying
a house was going to be out of reach for the vast majority. The median home price is around
$400,000, with many newer homes creeping up towards the half-million mark in desirable
districts. But the average income hovers around $80,000. That means it’s likely to take years
of scrupulous savings to get anywhere close to a down payment. Especially if you’re renting.
Fortunately, you don’t have to pay it all up front.
In the 1980s, the ratio of income to house prices sat at an affordable 3 to 1. Now,
it’s skyrocketed to 5 to 1. Because home prices are so detached from reality, the traditional
path to ownership is broken. The median down payment is just under 20%, leaving buyers
stuck with an average mortgage rate hovering around 7%. This means the average homeowner can
surrender around a third of monthly income while the interest means the sum will keep on growing.
For many, it’s not sustainable.
Financial advisors recommend keeping the percentage of gross income spent on
housing under a third. But between property taxes, insurance, and mortgage payments, it’s common for
it to creep up towards half of available money. This sparked a bizarre reverse housing crisis.
The scars of 2008 made traditional lenders so cautious, they shut regular buyers out of
the market. Compounding the disaster, the U.S. has been chronically under-building
houses for over a decade. The country now has a deficit of millions of homes. Labor shortages,
onerous zoning and land-use regulations, and the cost of land has paralyzed developers.
And the cost was passed on to consumers.
The Federal Reserve kept interest rates at historic lows from 2009 to 2022,
aiding in the recovery from both the financial crisis and later Covid-19.
That meant buyers could afford higher-priced homes without their mortgage surging month
to month. Because those existing homeowners are locked in, house prices refuse to drop.
Even as rates surge. The market is frozen. And it means a new generation of buyers are
forced to subsidize the lucky few who are tied into the deal of a lifetime.
For homeowners, it’s a nightmare.
For corporations, it’s an opportunity.
Over the last decade, rhetoric has increased over fears that the available homes are being
snapped up by corporate interests. They’re either being turned into rental houses in neighborhoods,
or hoarded until someone rich enough to afford them comes along. But this is overstated. These
institutional investors typically only own about 2-3% of actual housing stock,
and focus heavily on starter homes. And a lot of those are already foreclosed. Small-scale
investors, those owning 2-10 properties, make up to a quarter of the housing stock. And
this shadow has surged ever since short-term rental companies like Airbnb became popular.
But now, something else is happening.
And it has the potential to get a lot of people into their dream homes.
D.R. Horton has been in business as a home construction company since 1978,
but its portfolio keeps growing. It currently operates in 36 states and is ranked as the 120th
largest company in the United States. It’s held its position as the top homebuilder in the country
since 2002, but it’s not the only game in town. Florida-based Lennar is nipping at its heels.
D. R. Horton brags that they provide in-house financial services along with
home purchases under one roof. You can buy your house, and then get mortgage,
title, and insurance without ever leaving Horton’s office. Their dedicated subsidiary,
DHI Mortgage, offers competitive mortgage rates that can be pitched to clients the second they’re
interested in a house. There’s no need to go through a bank. This cuts through a lot of
the challenges of getting a bank to agree to a mortgage for someone with a middle-class income.
It also means the company can set its own terms.
Millennials and Gen Z have been stuck in an economy where it often feels like the price of
everything keeps on rising but their wages don’t rise with them. Most of them are still renting,
paying a third to half of their monthly income just to keep a roof over their heads,
and struggling to make ends meet. When they do save enough for a down payment
and go to the bank to discuss a mortgage, it feels like the game is rigged against
them. Their credit record isn’t sufficient. Somehow their steady rent payments aren’t
proof enough that they can pay a monthly mortgage. It starts to feel hopeless.
And that’s where the big guns step in.
D. R. Horton and Lennar have created a system where they can maintain control
of the process from the very first step to the last signing. With their deep pockets,
they can overcome the high cost of land and get the space they need to keep building homes.
They can oversee their own construction, not having to rely on third parties to
tell the truth about whether a home is solid enough to sell. And when people come looking,
they can refer them to their own financial services department instead of a bank.
And they’re motivated to make a sale.
What seems like an opportunity may actually be a trap.
While the mortgage loopholes that tripped up countless millennials and Gen Z seemed
unfair to many, the banks will tell you that it was for everyone’s good. The
2008 financial crisis partially happened because many people who never should have
been approved for a mortgage wound up in the hole. A healthy system protects everyone. It
keeps families from sinking their life savings into an economic death trap.
And it prevents a wave of foreclosures sweeping through the banking system.
But what does that matter when there’s money to make?
These powerful home-building organizations built captive in-house lending arms not just
to streamline things, but to approve as many clients as possible. Because while they’re
taking on all the risk of a deal, they’re taking on all the benefits as well. If they
handle the financial side of the deal, the house doesn’t go to a bank in the event of a
foreclosure. It goes right back to D. R. Horton or Lennar, ready to be fixed up and sold again.
And they have ways of making the deals make sense.
For most homebuyers, there are two big challenges. The first is the down payment,
which it can often take years to save for. While there can be negotiations over
the size of the down payment, with some offers getting as low as 10%,
the seller will usually insist on a sizable portion. And the other critical challenge
is the size of the mortgage payments, which can look intimidating at first.
But there are ways around that.
The most common way to make a challenging mortgage doable for a buyer is with a buydown. This is a
system where the seller offers an investment of their own into the mortgage as an incentive. They
usually contribute money into an escrow account that subsidizes the mortgage for a fixed period.
The most common method of this is a 2-1 buydown, where the first year offers a hefty subsidy,
and then it’s halved for the second year, and then it goes up to the standard amount for the
third year. While any lender can offer this, it can be a hard sell for a traditional mortgage
from a bank. It’ll immediately show that the buyer might have trouble meeting the payments.
But these large corporations don’t have that hesitation.
The major homebuilding corporations give out these incentives like candy,
with approximately 73% of D. R. Horton homebuyers receiving a rate buydown. By comparison,
around 67% of all US homebuilders offered a similar incentive. While not all homebuilders
offer financial services directly, it’s part of a significant trend in the industry. If
you’re not offering the same deal as your competitors, you wind up being
left behind. So even those who don’t offer full financial services can offer subsidies.
And they’re ready to shell out some big money.
Imagine if you were buying a car, and the dealer wasn’t willing to let you walk out the
door without a deal. You look at the car loan terms and you’re worried about meeting them,
so you decide to keep saving. But instead of letting you walk away, the dealer pulls out his
checkbook, writes a check, and presses it into your hand. He wants to sell you a car so badly,
he’s willing to pay off some of your loan. You’d probably think it was too good to be
true. But that’s exactly what’s happening to seven out of ten homebuyers in today’s economy.
Those incentives add up quickly.
According to data from fiscal year 2025, Lennar has been especially generous towards
its homebuyers. The average customer walks away from a deal with the massive
homebuilding company with incentives and buydowns averaging $62,700. That
averages out to 13.8% of Lennar’s total revenue… and it’s climbing.
Back in 2023, the average was only 8.8% of their total revenue. The
average homebuyer is walking away with an incentive that’s larger than the median
salary of the average worker in the United States… just to sign on the bottom line.
So why are these companies so invested in getting people to buy houses?
There’s an ugly secret to the US economy that companies are starting to figure out.
Their goal is usually profits above all. They raise prices when they can,
and avoid raising salaries as long as they can. But that only works if people
can still afford what they’re selling. The United States is primarily a consumer
country. If the people are too broke to buy, the corporate empire collapses.
So, to stop the home market bottoming out, because millennials and Gen Z are stuck in a debt trap,
the companies need to make it easier to buy.
And they did.
But now history may be repeating itself.
Behind every mortgage buydown is a ticking clock,
and one that comes sooner than expected for many people.
Buydown subsidizes the mortgage, allowing people to save up and get their footing
in their new home before the full bill comes down. But it comes due all the same. Currently,
both DHI and Lennar are looking at their current holdings, and seeing serious warning
signs. The number of mortgage-holders who are underwater is skyrocketing,
and it all comes back to the large group of mortgages given out between 2022 and 2024.
This is when the rates exploded, and people are now feeling the walls close in. Currently,
20.8% of DHI Mortgage loans from this period are underwater.
Lennar has even worse results, with 30.7% of their loans being in danger of foreclosure.
That means no one is the winner here.
When a loan is “underwater”, that means the owner owes more to the bank - in this case,
the homebuilding corporation - than the home could sell for on the open market. When this happens,
even foreclosure isn’t a solution. D. R. Horton or Lennar could reclaim the home,
but could they fully recoup their money from doing so?
A massive surge in foreclosures could cause big problems for the housing market just like it did
in 2005. So the lenders have an interest in keeping people in their new houses as well.
But the math is getting harder and harder to square.
Right now, the housing market is producing grim results for many people. With the current median
household income coming in at just over $83,700, the average monthly payment comes in at $3,700,
a whopping 53% of average income. Many people find themselves in a no-win situation. If they
pay their mortgage on time, they often have to max out their credit cards in order to make ends
meet. But if they start falling behind on their mortgage, it might be impossible to catch up.
And maybe the only way to win is not to play.
To make matters worse, the government gutted the last remaining safety net for homeowners.
Overhauls to the tax code have effectively wiped out the rebates families used to
survive mortgages. Today, the mortgage interest deduction has dropped to measly $69 a month in
average tax relief. The majority of Americans don’t get any benefit, forcing them to opt for
the standard deduction instead. And at current interest rates, anyone who actually manages to
pay off their mortgage will end up handing the bank more than double the value of the house.
So renters might come out on top.
Renting doesn’t feel particularly good, because you’re giving over
a large percentage of your income to someone else. But technically,
mortgage holders are doing the same. And because of regulations in many major cities,
landlords are limited in how much they can raise the rent each year. It can actually be harder to
evict a renter than it is to foreclose on a home. It usually takes up to 7 years for
buying a home to even be a better financial deal over renting, because of the high initial costs.
And there’s one other big factor - flexibility.
Renters are always prepared to shift things around. A sudden rent hike can lead to someone
being forced to move. So they pack up and find a new place. There’s no long-term sunk cost,
only a new landlord. By contrast, a homeowner can put hundreds of thousands of dollars into their
house for years, lose their job, and lose the house with little hope of seeing the money again.
For the companies behind the current boom, that could be very bad news.
Right now, both D. R. Horton and Lennar are still dominating in the homebuilding market. Horton has
a generally good reputation, but Lennar has found itself in the headlines for all the wrong reasons.
They’ve been accused of cutting serious corners in their homebuilding, with many of their newly
built houses being found to suffer from major issues like cracked foundations and leaking
windows. The company’s solution? To force homeowners to sign NDAs when making repairs.
Those windows may not be the only thing springing a leak.
Right now, both companies are starting to see the consequences of over-leveraging their
homebuyers. They’ve taken on customers who banks would have turned down,
offering them the deal of a lifetime to sign on the dotted line. The result is
overleveraged homeowners who might not be able to keep up on their mortgages. If they
start defaulting en masse, the companies will wind up with more stock than they
know what to do with. Their only hope will be finding new homeowners to repeat the cycle.
But will the fish be biting this time?
The difference between millennials and Gen Z is that millennials saw a world filled with
the things their parents told them were the American dream. They’ve been striving
for it ever since. But Gen Z didn’t grow up in that world, and they don’t see the appeal
in chasing the same thing. For many of them, renting is just the standard way of things,
and they’re less likely to take the big swings needed to buy a home. And that
might leave these massive corporations amid a sea of homes, with no one to sell them to.
Could the bottom be about to fall out of the economy…again? Check out “This
Is What Always Happens Before a Market Crash” or watch this.
